topic: putting a crooked saddle right: girth webs, felted flocking and twice yearly adjustment

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-4)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: pressure mat (mata pomiarowa saddle fittera); referent zwyczajny procesowy zakotwiczony poza rozmowa

base: My old saddle has begun to sit crooked on the mare and rub her withers.
A newer saddle hangs on the same rack and sits level on her back.
A pressure mat lies beside them and records what happens under the panels during a ride.
The flocking in the old one feels lumpy on the left and thin on the right.
Should I have it reflocked, or check the girth straps and the tree first?
Check the tree and the girth straps before anyone touches the flocking at all.
A broken tree or a torn web will pull a saddle sideways every single time.
New flocking over a twisted tree simply hides the fault for a few months.
Stand behind the horse and look down the gullet while the girth is done up.
The tree seems sound and the gullet looks straight when I sight down it.
One girth strap, though, has pulled loose from its stitching at the webbing.
The pressure mat shows a hard band under the left panel through the whole ride.
Would that loose strap alone explain the saddle drifting to one side under me?
A loose strap alone will do it, because the girth then pulls unevenly forward.
Have the webbing restitched onto the tree by a saddler who works with a hand awl.
The hard band under the left panel is a separate matter and needs flocking work.
Deal with the strap first, then let the flocking be adjusted to the settled shape.
The saddler restitched both webs and the saddle now sits square at the halt.
Ridden out, it still slips a little left, though far less than before.
The newer saddle never slips at all, even on the same long hill work.
Is the remaining drift the lumpy flocking, or is my own seat crooked?
It is most likely the flocking, since lumps hold the panel off the muscle.
Ask the saddler to open the panels and tease the old wool apart by hand.
Adding new wool onto lumps is the commonest shortcut and it never lasts long.
Ride for a fortnight afterwards before you judge whether your seat plays any part.
The panels were opened and the wool inside had felted into two hard pads.
Fresh wool went in evenly and the saddle has stayed square for two weeks.
The mare stretches her neck down now, which she never did last autumn.
How often should the flocking be checked before it felts into pads again?
Have it looked at twice a year, once in spring and once in autumn.
Wool settles fastest in the first three months after any panel has been opened.
A horse changes shape with the seasons as well, especially one in hard work.
Small adjustments twice yearly cost far less than one full reflock every third year.
That makes sense, and the mare has certainly filled out over the summer grass.
Her back is broader than it was when the saddle was last adjusted.
I can already feel the gullet sitting closer to her spine than before.
Is that something flocking can answer, or does the tree need widening now?
Flocking cannot answer a narrow gullet, because the tree sets that width outright.
A saddler can open the head plate a size on most modern trees.
Older trees will not take it and are better sold on than forced wider.
Measure her again in late winter, when the summer condition has gone off her.
